results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
*Digital Compositing for Film and Video* describes two ways to build your own chroma keyer — a simple HSV/color-curve version and a 3D color-space version — and then cautions that a homemade keyer is probably more hassle than it's worth [S2].

**What a chroma keyer does.** A chroma keyer internally converts the RGB image to HSV or HSL first, because saturation is not an RGB attribute. You set a starting pixel value as the "center" of the key, then define ranges for hue, saturation, and value; pixels inside those ranges go white, pixels outside go black, and tolerance settings are what give the key soft edges [S14]. At its most basic, it means picking a range of colors and defining every pixel in that range as background [S3]. The book also flags terminology chaos here: many people call every keyer a "chroma keyer," but most greenscreen tools (Keylight, Ultimatte) are actually color difference keyers, while Primatte is a sophisticated three-dimensional chroma keyer [S4].

**Simple method: HSV + color curves.** Start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV, then pipe the HSV image into a color curve. Since the RED curve now carries Hue, the GREEN curve carries Saturation, and the BLUE curve carries Value (brightness), you adjust the three curves to include or exclude the target's hue, saturation, and value ranges [S1]. The book frames this as an instructive exercise rather than a production tool, and it points to a test image, *Chroma key target.tif*, for practicing keys on various parts of a picture [S5].

**3D variation: keying in the RGB color cube.** A second, "interesting and flexible variation" works on utterly different principles: rather than converting to HSV, it plots colors in the RGB color cube and builds a key for any arbitrary color, as a grossly simplified version of Primatte's approach [S8]. The recipe is an equation where R1G1B1 is the normalized center color you want to isolate and R2G2B2 is the normalized value of each pixel; you enter it in a math node or expression format your software supports, with *greenscreen.tiff* provided as a test plate [S13].

**The book's verdict.** Unlike the DIY luma keyer, where being clever can yield substantial improvements over the basic version, a homemade chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than it's worth" — worth trying once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon [S2]. That's consistent with how the sources describe the gap: real keyers add tolerance controls for soft edges [S14], and modern tools like DaVinci Resolve's Delta keyer extract mattes with more sophisticated color difference methods instead of simple hue-and-saturation ranges [S6].

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
A nonsquare pixel is one whose width does not equal its height — rectangular rather than square — and the ratio of width to height is what the book calls the **pixel aspect ratio** [S3][S4][S7]. On a properly adjusted computer monitor every pixel is square, so its pixel aspect ratio is 1:1 [S1]. Nonsquare systems arise whenever the aspect ratio of the displayed image differs from that of the original digital image [S2]. The pixel aspect ratio is independent of the image's own aspect ratio: analog NTSC video, for instance, uses a pixel aspect ratio of 10:11, meaning its pixels are slightly taller than they are wide [S14][S7].

Because film output has no identifiable pixels, the book uses different terminology for cinema: film formats that optically distort an image are called **squeezed**, and formats representing images with distorted aspect ratios are called **anamorphic** — a term borrowed from art, describing a distorted image that can be restored to its original shape [S13]. The most common anamorphic format, Cinemascope, serves as the running example because its 2:1 squeeze is the most dramatic [S6]. Outside film, standard-definition video uses rectangular pixels (720 × 480 NTSC-DV and 720 × 576 PAL-DV), whereas HD, graphics software, and computer monitors use square pixels [S9]. When a system temporarily "unsqueezes" an image for viewing, it's said to display nonsquare pixels, but the pixels on the monitor still appear properly proportioned — only the display is transformed, never the underlying image data [S5].

The author's stance is practical and cautionary: nonsquare-pixel formats demand special consideration because naive operations introduce visible errors [S6]. Two problems get particular attention. Rotating an element while it's still squeezed distorts the result; the correct workflow is to unsqueeze it, rotate, and then resqueeze along the x-axis, and even a subtle 5° rotation leaves a visible error, so the advice is to double-check everything when working with nonsquare pixels [S10]. Likewise, a digitally created perfect circle sent straight to NTSC video appears as an ellipse stretched 11/10 vertically; you may need to scale manually to compensate, though many systems automate the step and you should know how your particular setup behaves [S14].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The "Miscellaneous Drawing Tips" sections in Glebas's *Directing the Story* are a checklist of short craft maxims that keep drawings readable, expressive, and energetic [S2][S5]. In full, they cover:

**Clarity and communication**
- Draw for clarity — one idea per sketch; draw attention to one idea at a time, just like when speaking, and make sure your drawings say what you think they're saying [S2][S6].
- Have something to say in your image; don't doodle [S2].
- You should be able to blacken in your drawings and still read what is happening — keep decoration within the main outline so drawings don't get busy, and make sure outlines are interesting [S1].
- Don't get too clever; tricky camera angles often just make the drawing ambiguous [S5].

**Dynamics and pose**
- Avoid symmetry — it's boring and makes drawings look cut out; use angles and dynamic asymmetry instead [S5].
- Play straight lines against curves for interest; use straight line symbols for stretches and bent line symbols for squashes [S2][S5].
- Draw bold and expressive [S5].
- Watch the body's landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S5].

**Feeling and purpose**
- Show how the character feels: feel the pose and the emotion in your body as you draw [S5].
- A person is always "doing" something — express the purpose and feel the pose kinetically [S5].
- When drawing eyes, darken pupils [S2].

**Process**
- Don't be afraid to redraw; search for the best solution to tell the story [S2].
- If part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and rework it [S2].
- Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S2].
- Follow Vance Gerry's workflow test: "If you can't photocopy it, trace it. If you can't trace it, then you'll have to draw it" [S7].

The through-line is that every tip serves the story: clarity first, then expressiveness, with the subject's purpose and feeling highlighted and everything else subordinated to that idea [S5][S6].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The VES Handbook of Visual Effects answers this with a decision rule: the choice between transcoding and color rerendering depends on how dissimilar the two displays are — specifically their black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma [S1][S2].

**Transcoding** is a purely mechanical re-encoding. If the displays share black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma, and differ only in primary chromaticities, the encoded colors can be transcoded by linearizing the first display's encoded RGB values, converting them to CIE XYZ, converting those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, and reimposing the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. No appearance decision is made; the image is simply re-encoded in new display coordinates [S2].

**Color rerendering** is a perceptual re-render. When contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar, the best solution is color rerendering: any color rendering implicitly or explicitly done for the first display is undone, and the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are then color rendered for the second display [S1]. In color science, color rendering means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment [S4] — for example, a still camera JPEG color-rendered for a sunlit desert scene must be re-rendered for an office monitor with far lower peak white [S4].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When used** | Displays differ mainly in primaries; same levels, gamma, viewing conditions [S2] | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions grossly dissimilar [S1] |
| **What changes** | Signal encoding only — same appearance [S2] | Perceptual appearance, viewing-environment compensation [S1][S4] |
| **Pipeline** | Linearize RGB₁ → XYZ → RGB₂ → re-encode [S2] | Undo rendering for display A → XYZ → render for display B [S1] |

The context that makes this concrete: output-referred encodings like Adobe RGB and sRGB are already color rendered for a display environment, while camera raw is not — raw encodings must be color rendered downstream, which is easier for a VFX team to do than to undo rendering the camera baked in [S4][S6]. The ACES workflow institutionalizes the rerendering half of this: the RRT is the standardized color-appearance rendering for dark-surround theatrical viewing [S3][S5], and ODTs adapt that RRT-derived look to each specific display device, with gamut mapping still needed for low-gamut displays like HDTV [S9]. The RRT is meant to stay stable and universal, incorporating picture rendering for the viewing environment, while manufacturers supply their own ODTs [S15].

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The book's core claim is that affect, fatigue, and injury are **control states**: persistent conditions that must change later action selection and execution — "not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen" [S3]. For cinematic characters, this means the states have to shape what the character does next, not merely describe how the finished performance feels.

## How the book defines each state

**Affect** sits at Layer B of the layered representation: a continuous trajectory over valence, arousal, and dominance/control, answering whether the character's experience is becoming more positive or negative, activated or calm, empowered or overwhelmed [S1]. It is updated through an appraisal mechanism — a trigger with goal-congruence, controllability, and certainty scores moves a prior state to a posterior and yields concrete behavioral effects. In the handbook's interception example, a failed expectation narrows attention toward the exit lane, makes recovery urgent but less mechanically clean, and raises risk tolerance for one recovery attempt [S3].

The central argument for affect is **underdetermination**: it is useful for interpolation and temporal arcs, but the same high-arousal negative state can be portrayed as fear, anger, pain, or disgust depending on appraisal, context, and action tendencies [S1]. The book therefore rejects deterministic mappings such as "anger = always faster" or "fear = always retreat," since research supports kinematic cues to emotion only at population level, with character, culture, task, injury, and tactical intent as moderators [S11].

**Fatigue** is modeled as an accumulator: f(r, t+Δt) = clamp(f(r, t) + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1), where f is fatigue rather than remaining capacity, and the work/impact/recovery terms must be calibrated because prose alone cannot tell you their values [S4]. It decomposes into global exertion (RPE 0–10, breath cycle, recovery rate) and local capacity (per-limb values such as left_leg 0.46), with coordination effects like increased step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, and greater trunk contribution when a shoulder is taxed [S5].

**Injury** is a persistent object with mechanical consequences and compensations: region, pain and severity ratings, load-acceptance and flexion-tolerance factors, and behaviors like favoring the right leg or shortening the left stance interval — plus an explicit uncertainty field, because the source is dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement [S6]. Persistence is enforced in the specimen fight IR: Mara's shoulder injury begins at state.v2 and continues through the final frame, and no action boundary may discard support, root velocity, orientation, injury, ownership, or active contact [S10].

## Why control states must be observable

The handbook operationalizes "control state" into failure-checkable metrics, so a cinematic performance can be audited for whether the states actually controlled action [S2]:

| Metric | What it verifies | Failure state |
|---|---|---|
| Affect-to-action coupling | Declared affect has a visible or tactical consequence | Emotion appears only in label or face |
| Fatigue propagation | Taxed regions alter later capacity, variability, timing, or tactics | Exertion never changes later action |
| Injury compensation consistency | Declared mechanical effects and compensations persist | Injured region performs at baseline without cause |

Two adjacent corpus sources round out the picture. Stage Combat Arts adds physiological detail to the injury state: pain alters breath and voice, injuries near the body's center lower vocal pitch while peripheral injuries raise it, and adrenalin can mask the extent of an injury [S9]. The Laban-based materials use "state" in a different sense — the six Effort states are movement configurations combining two motion factors (mobile, stable, remote, rhythm, dream, awake) — a vocabulary of expressive movement rather than the handbook's control-state semantics [S7][S8][S12][S15].

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The book treats an object moving against a background as a designed composition, governed by three visual factors: the direction of the line or track traced by the moving object, the orientation or angle of the background's linear motif, and the **contrast or affinity** created by combining the foreground object's track with the background's linear motif [S11]. The foreground path and the background's dominant lines are meant to be read together, not independently.

This sits inside a broader theory of movement. Anything that moves in relation to the frame line is a moving object, and every moving object generates a track — the path of its movement — which is categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed [S6]. Relative movement occurs when one object's motion is gauged by its changing position against a second, stationary object [S4]. But the book also describes a subtler phenomenon: in its forest example, a car drives in a circle while the camera pans to follow it, so the car stays fixed in the frame; the trees sweeping in the opposite direction of the pan generate **apparent movement**, and the viewer transfers that movement to the car, even though there is no actual relative movement [S10].

Two techniques extend this. **Induced movement** lets a moving object transfer its movement to a nearby stationary one, making the stationary object appear to move [S2]. And during 2D and 3D camera moves, the speed of foreground, midground, and background objects reads distinctly because camera movement is transferred to everything in front of the lens [S12]. The effect of all this is perceptual: a background's motion can reveal a subject's motion that the frame alone would hide, and the alignment or clash between an object's track and the background's linear structure produces visual continuity or visual tension [S10][S11].

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
In the books referenced here, sound editing is the postproduction craft of building a film's entire aural universe — and it is consistently described as the element on which the believability (and therefore the success) of the picture ultimately rests [S1][S11].

## What sound editing is

A film's **sound design** is defined as an aural world made of layered tracks: dialogue, sound effects, music, ambient sounds (atmospheres), and sometimes voice-overs [S9]. The **sound designer** is responsible for the audience's overall acoustic experience — a role the sources compare to the director of photography's for picture — and oversees the many individual tracks, which include dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley sounds [S2]. The **sound effects editor** then places each effect into its corresponding track, working with effects grouped into four main categories; the retrieved text states the four-category rule but does not enumerate the categories themselves [S3]. Whatever production did not capture in original sound is created during this phase [S1].

## How the sound edit proceeds

The workflow is staged. During the rough cut, only the soundtracks needed for dramatic decisions are edited — typically dialogue and occasional scratch music — and the full multi-track design is built only after picture lock, one track at a time: usually between 6 and 16 tracks for simple films, and up to 60 tracks in a feature [S9][S14]. Dialogue editing is completed first; the creative sound work begins after it [S2]. The assembled elements are synced to picture, grouped in their own tracks, equalized, and mixed down to a master — stereo at the simplest, 5.1 surround for cinema [S9]. Dancyger adds that the sound edit demands more decisions than the picture edit because a wrong decision can readily undermine the visuals [S1]. Core techniques include fading one effect out as another fades up for smooth sound-to-sound transitions, and carrying one continuous sound across two disparate visuals, which implies a link between shots or scenes — so the mix can separate or connect scenes and imply either the passage or the continuity of time [S14]. Editors may also manipulate speed and pitch during the edit [S4], and tools such as DaVinci Resolve's Fairlight page are designed precisely for this kind of placement, with clip-speed changes used for advanced pitch and sound-design effects [S6].

## Goals and principles

Two principles anchor the whole enterprise: **narrative clarity** and **believability**. Because sound is processed more rapidly than visuals, any sound that seems unbelievable undermines the images and destroys audience involvement; believable sound is therefore the most urgent goal of the sound edit [S11]. The rough sound edit seeks believability of performance and a progressive sense of story, matching the rough picture edit, while dramatic emphasis and metaphor are deferred to the fine cut [S12]. The editor's first task is determining the narrative point of the scene and supporting — or "surrounding" — it with sound; Gillo Pontecorvo's *The Battle of Algiers* is cited as a case where authenticity in sound is central to the story's power [S1]. The broader rationale is that sound affects audiences on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels, which is why "silent" films were never actually silent — music always accompanied them once technology allowed [S8]. Care in building and mixing sound tracks matters at every scale, from a two-track music video to a blockbuster with 62 or more tracks [S7]. One historical caution from Dancyger: in the early sound era, editing itself was inhibited, because dialogue recorded on disk or Movietone could not be cut without losing sync; only after rerecording and multiple-camera shooting became common did editing regain its freedom [S15].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The core rule in *Hey Whipple, Squeeze This* is blunt: **underwrite**. Sullivan calls overwriting "the most common mistake people make in radio" and tells writers to "be a genius. Underwrite" [S4]. Sparse writing is the book's default for the medium — unless the concept itself demands a lot of words and fast action, everything else should be cut down [S2].

The practical technique the book offers:

- **Time out the mandatories first.** If a spot has to end with legal copy or a promotional tag, write that as sparely as possible and time it — what's left is the space your commercial must fit in [S1] [S4]. A :60 is a house, a :30 is a tent; tags and tags eat into the total time, so write sparely from the start [S1].
- **Cover the wall with concepts, not scripts.** Generate lots of ideas by scribbling the general concept on Post-its before writing any full script [S3].
- **Write one spot at a time.** Since radio has no visual graphic standards, you can attack the brief spot by spot; as long as everything is written to one strategy, the separate spots add up to one brand [S9].

The payoff of spare writing is in the performance: it lets the voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time, and it creates silence — the book's favorite idea — which is to radio what white space is to print: "Silence enlarges the idea it surrounds" [S2] [S12]. The book also treats radio as pure writing since there's no imagery to lean on — creative director Rosann Calisi is quoted calling radio writers "gold because that's writing in its most pure form" [S8] — and the medium's canvas is actually the listener's imagination, where impossible, unaffordable visuals are free [S11]. Against that power, Sullivan warns away from the tired formats: fake game shows, fake call-in shows, fake newscasts, "I'm here at…" openers, Don Pardo-isms, and over-the-top cartoon voices [S6].

The same principle echoes in the other corpus books: Rabiger's directing text says overwritten dialogue is repetitive and that the best cinema dialogue is highly succinct yet informally accurate, keeping the characters' idiosyncrasies while cutting the redundancy [S7] [S14], and *Building a StoryBrand* frames it in one line — the key to great writing isn't what you say, it's what you don't say [S13].
